analysis:
Examined SSDWholeRootMaintainer.swift base and head, plus the new tests in SSDPrefixCacheTests.swift. The change caches per-root header-readability verdicts keyed by path and lstat identity (dev, ino, size, mtime, ctime with nanoseconds). The cache is consulted only when the fanout directory chain still passes the safety checks (isSafeModelRoot, pathResolvesToItself, isRealDirectory, openDirectoryChain). A header read is skipped only for an unchanged identity. Failed reads are never remembered, so a transient failure cannot keep an owned block past its TTL (T-041 TTL/LRU bounds preserved).

Tampering check: a ctime change forces a re-read. Rewriting content with a restored mtime still changes ctime, and the new test covers that case. Replacement changes the inode or ctime. A ctime-preserving attacker would need root or clock manipulation, which is outside the operator-local trust assumptions for T-041 and does not meaningfully weaken the ownership proof. Even if a stale verdict were reused, deletion still goes through removeItemIfSafe and the epoch/budget barriers, so the only effect is deleting an exact-grammar lookalike file inside the dedicated cache root. No new data exposure, no new I/O surface, no change to crypto or lookup tags.

Integration notes: the identity is taken before the read, so a race resolves to a re-read on the next pass. readableHeaderIdentities is guarded by maintenanceLock because ownedContents is only called inside maintain. The map is replaced each pass by a defer, so it stays bounded to the files currently seen. The stale-verdict window is one pass at most. Early return on an unsafe root does not update the map (the defer is placed after the guard), which is harmless. Tests are test-only. No threat-model update needed; the T-041 cleanup guarantees are unchanged.
